chapter: Los Angeles 1947-48, Rock Island and bebop in New York
title: Leaving the Horseshoe: the policemen at the bar and the 'Slippery Tit'
summary: Three men at the bar ask whether he'd rather be called 'Nigger' or 'darky'; he declines to fight and goes back to Bellson's.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: The name of the club was what?

[Alborn's] Horseshoe. A bandstand behind the bar, you know, at the end of the bar. It wasn't a circular bar. And a nice little bandstand, good acoustics, a nice band. I sure hated to see it go the way it did. Well, in the meanwhile, Buddy de Franco and Louis had received wires to rejoin Tommy Dorsey in Miami, Florida. For rehearsals. But they didn't send for Charlie because they didn't want Charlie in the South, and he was supposed to rejoin the band someplace else. So while we're in Chicago, Hank and Buddy leaves. And we come back, there's no-one there but Ike and Charlie and I. So now we've got to get a local drummer and a local piano player. So I guess we played about three tunes and the bartender comes up to me and he says, 'John, there's three gentlemen back here wants you to have a drink with them when you're finished.' Well, I went back to pay my respects, you know. I didn't expect what I ran into, because I got all my drinks free. There wasn't any point in my going back there, but I called myself being sociable, you know, and as I approached them they said, 'First, which would you rather be called? Nigger or darky?'

My feathers fell. I said, "Well, at this point, I wouldn't advise you to call me anything." Because if this had been in New York, I know what I would have done. I would have thrown a punch across the bar, and that's what they were hoping that I would do, you know antagonize me into doing something wrong, where they could shoot me down. Because I understand one of these policemen had killed a serviceman for urinating in the alley because he wasn't ten feet off the streets. The soldier wasn't too bad, because I told him I'd come in from the other end. But he killed him, you know. So I said, "Well," I said, "I'll have a Slippery Tit." And for those of you who aren't acquainted with this particular drink, it's composed of tequila, vodka and gin, three shotglasses, individually. And the bartender said, "We don't have any tequila." I said, "Well, supplement that with some Canadian Club." So I said, "Make that a Slippery Dick Nixon." You know, that was before his time, but you know, Tricky Dick? Richard, nicknamed Dick. So I drank the three drinks, I walked around the bandstand, got my bass, went downstairs, put the cover on it, gathered up my wet shirts that I had produced, you know, by being on the bandstand, perspiring, letting them dry out so I could launder them the next day. I gathered up all of my belongings, walked from there to Mr. Bellson's house. I'm not supposed to be there, but there wasn't anywhere else for me to go but there.
